title: How McDonald's Really Makes Money
the_thought: The thicker check is the rent, not the royalty.
hook: The tray hits the window. A paper bag. A cup. A handful of change. McDonald's just sold a meal. The till at the window made a noise. That noise is not how the Corporation got paid. The thicker check is the rent, not the royalty. So where did the money go?

levels.name: The Tray
beats: Watch the window for one ordinary night. Cars crawl under a bright canopy. A teen in a hoodie reads a blank board, pays, takes a bag, and drives off. It feels like the whole company just rang a sale. That is the costume. The person who handed over the cash paid the restaurant. The restaurant is usually somebody else's. Fiscal 2025 filings say McDonald's had 45,356 restaurants at year end, across more than 100 countries. About 95 percent of those restaurants were franchised. In the United States the mix was about 95 percent franchised. In the International Operated Markets it was about 89 percent. In the International Developmental Licensed Markets it was about 99 percent. The guest still sees one system. The cash does not. The 10-K is blunt about why the Company still runs some restaurants itself. Directly operating restaurants, it says, helps it act as a credible franchisor. Company kitchens are where standards get tested. They are where crew methods get practiced. They are not the main cash register. Keep that in your head when the bag hits the seat. You paid for food. You did not settle the headquarters invoice. Systemwide sales are the total of every restaurant, Company-owned and franchised. In fiscal 2025 those Systemwide sales were 139.4 billion dollars, up 7 percent, or 5 percent in constant currencies. That is the number people point at when they say the golden arches print money. It is a real number. It is also not the Corporation's revenue line. Franchised sales in that same year were 129.675 billion dollars. The filing says those franchised sales are not recorded as revenues by the Company. Management still watches them, because rent and royalties are calculated from them, and because they show whether franchisees are healthy. The guest's tray lives on that 129.675 billion line. The Corporation does not book it. So the first mystery is simple enough for a child and rude enough for an adult. If almost every restaurant is someone else's, and if most of the tray never becomes McDonald's revenue, what invoice does headquarters actually send? Hold the bag. We are going to open the envelope. The drive-thru is not a lie. Nearly 29,000 drive-thru locations existed globally in the 2025 report, including more than 95 percent of the roughly 13,700 United States restaurants. Convenience is the product the guest buys. Convenience is not the product the Corporation invoices. The operator who signed the deal is standing somewhere behind that canopy, and that operator is the customer the But why does that change the invoice? 10-K keeps talking around. Two million people work in franchised restaurants. The Corporation itself employed over 150,000 at year end 2025, and about 70 percent of those Company employees sat outside the United States. Most of the faces at the window do not work for the listed company. They work for the person who pays the rent. That is not a slogan. It is the ownership structure. The tray is loud. The invoice is quiet. We are following the quiet one. One more beat before we leave the window. The filing says fees vary by type of site, by how much the Company invested, and by local conditions. There is no single folk number on every lease. There is a pattern. Conventional sites send rent and royalty. Licensed sites send royalty. Company sites send the whole ticket and the whole But why does that change the invoice? cost. If a narrator collapses those three into one vibe, the rest of the video is decoration.

levels.name: Two Totals
beats: Put two machines on a table. One machine is labeled Systemwide. It rang 139.4 billion dollars in fiscal 2025. The other machine is labeled Corporation. It rang 26.885 billion dollars of consolidated revenue. Same year. Same brand. Different jobs. If you line those two totals up, consolidated revenue was about 19 dollars for every 100 dollars of Systemwide sales. That is a blended average from the 10-K, not the fee on a typical ticket in Ohio. Do not turn it into a folk tax. It is a flashlight. It shows how much of the tray the listed company is even allowed to record. Inside the 26.885 billion, the pieces are not equal. Revenues from franchised restaurants were 16.548 billion dollars. Sales by Company-owned and operated restaurants were 9.690 billion dollars. Other revenues were 647 million dollars. Other revenues, the filing says, But why does that change the invoice? are mostly fees paid by franchisees to recover a portion of technology and digital costs, plus brand licensing for packaged goods. The app is not the engine. It is a recovery line and a convenience layer. Now look at the 9.690 billion of Company-operated sales. That is the full till of the restaurants the Corporation still runs. Food, paper, payroll, occupancy. In the same year, Company-owned and operated restaurant expenses were 8.268 billion dollars. The restaurant-level margin on that fleet was 1.422 billion dollars. Real money. Small next to what comes next. Franchised restaurant margins were 13.930 billion dollars in fiscal 2025. The filing says franchised margins represented approximately 90 percent of restaurant margin dollars. Company-operated margins were the remaining sliver. Headquarters can live without ringing the tray. It cannot live without the franchise invoice. Operating income was 12.393 billion But why does that change the invoice? dollars. Operating margin, defined as operating income divided by total revenues, was 46.1 percent, up from 45.2 percent in 2024. That looks like a software company until you remember the 46.1 percent is not taken from Systemwide sales. It is taken from the 26.885 billion the Corporation is allowed to book. A 46 percent operating margin on the invoice is not a 46 percent tax on the guest. Cash provided by operations was 10.6 billion dollars in fiscal 2025, up 1.1 billion from the prior year. Capital expenditures were 3.4 billion dollars, mostly new openings and some reinvestment. Free cash flow was 7.2 billion dollars. The 10-K also says the Company opened 2,276 restaurants and closed 396 in 2025. The System, including developmental licensees and affiliates, opened nearly 2,300. Growth is a lot of new keys. We will get to But why does that change the invoice? the keys. For the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, global Systemwide sales were 37 billion dollars, up 5 percent, or 4 percent in constant currencies. Revenues from franchised restaurants were 4.393 billion. Company-operated sales were 2.525 billion. Total revenues were 7.099 billion. Franchised margins were 3.713 billion and still about 90 percent of restaurant margin dollars. The split did not flip because the calendar flipped. Comparable sales in that quarter grew 1.3 percent globally, including 0.8 percent in the United States. The engine can grow slowly at the window and still send a thick invoice, as long as the operator is ringing enough sales to trigger rent and royalty. That is a different kind of growth than a grocer's membership door. This invoice rides on someone else's till. Two totals. 139.4 and 26.9. If you only watch the first But why does that change the invoice? machine, you think McDonald's sold every burger. If you watch the second, you start asking what, exactly, is inside the 16.548 billion of franchised revenue. That is the next envelope. Notice what is missing from the Corporation machine. Food cost on franchised shifts is missing. Crew wages on franchised shifts are missing. The operator's loan on the fryers is missing. Those costs are real. They live on someone else's books. Headquarters chose, in conventional markets, to live on the site invoice instead. That choice is the whole film.

levels.name: The Thicker Envelope
beats: Open the franchised revenue line the way the 10-K opens it. Fiscal 2025. Rents: 10.442 billion dollars. Royalties: 6.018 billion dollars. Initial fees: 88 million dollars. Add them and you get 16.548 billion. The rent stack is taller than the royalty stack. The thicker check is the rent, not the royalty. Say it again, because every copycat video wants this to be a vibe. It is a table. Rents were about 63 percent of franchised revenues that year. Royalties were the smaller branded slice. Initial fees were a rounding error next to either stack. The brand still matters. The brand is not the fatter check. The filing describes conventional franchisees with boring precision. They pay rent and royalties based upon a percent of sales, with specified minimum rent payments, plus initial fees when a restaurant opens or a franchise is granted. But why does that change the invoice? Rental income includes minimum rent, recognized straight-line over the term, and variable rent based on a percent of sales, recognized when the underlying sales occur. Royalty is a percent of sales when the sales occur. The Company does not publish one universal royalty rate in that 10-K. Do not invent one. The published fact is the mix: rent larger than royalty. Franchised occupancy expenses were 2.618 billion dollars. Those costs, the filing says, include lease expense and depreciation, because the Company generally owns or secures a long-term lease on the land and building. Franchised margin is franchised revenue minus that occupancy. 16.548 minus 2.618 is the 13.930 billion margin line. The Corporation is not paying the crew on those shifts. It is paying to keep control of the site, then invoicing the operator. Minimum rent is the floor. At December But why does that change the invoice? 31, 2025, future gross minimum rent payments due to the Company under existing conventional franchise arrangements totaled 31.451 billion dollars. That is not a forecast of next year's guest counts. It is contracted floor rent already sitting on signed deals, on owned sites and leased sites. Even if a slow week hits the window, a conventional operator still owes the floor. Variable rent and royalties still swing with sales. The floor is why the model is called stable in the filing's own language. This is the strange decision that makes sense. Headquarters could have charged only a brand royalty and let every operator own the dirt. Then the fatter check would not exist. Conventional McDonald's did the opposite in the markets where it wants site control. It kept the land and the building in the family, or locked a long lease, and charged rent that can grow with sales. The royalty still arrives. It just arrives thinner. Do not turn this into a morality play about landlords. The 10-K says the Company believes ownership of real estate, combined with franchisee co-investment, helps restaurant performance. The franchisee still buys the equipment, the signs, the seating, the decor. Both sides put chips on the table. One side keeps the dirt. If you swap the company name here and keep the two stacks, the video breaks. Visa's fee is a pulse on someone else's loan. Costco's membership is a card at a door. This invoice is a rent envelope that outgrew the royalty stamp inside one burger system. That is the only reason this chapter exists. Other revenues of 647 million dollars will tempt a narrator who wants a tech story. Franchisees pay But why does that change the invoice? to recover part of the cost of digital platforms. There is brand licensing for packaged food in grocery aisles. Trailing twelve-month Systemwide sales to loyalty members exceeded 40 billion dollars by the second quarter 2026 release, with nearly 220 million 90-day active users across 70 measured markets. Loyalty is a habit layer. It is not 10.442 billion of rent. Keep the envelope in the shot.

levels.name: Who Keeps The Key
beats: There is a brass key on a numbered tag. It is ugly on purpose. It does not look like a sandwich. In a conventional deal, that key is the story. The 10-K says conventional arrangements generally include a lease and a license. The franchisee gets the right to operate using the System, and in most cases the use of a restaurant facility, generally for 20 years. At the end of the 20 years, the Company maintains control of the underlying real estate and building. It can sign the same operator again. It can sign a different operator. It can close the restaurant. The key comes back. Franchisees generally pay property taxes, insurance, and site maintenance. They live in the building. They do not keep the building. That is the 20-year clock. It is not a biography of a founder. It is But why does that change the invoice? a contract the filing still bothers to explain because the whole cash-flow machine sits on it. As of December 31, 2025, the Company owned approximately 56 percent of the land and approximately 80 percent of the buildings for restaurants in its consolidated markets. Net property and equipment on the balance sheet was 28.241 billion dollars. Under franchise arrangements alone, net property and equipment was 22.8 billion dollars, including 7.1 billion of land, after 16.9 billion of accumulated depreciation. Those are not set decorations. They are why the rent stack can exist. The Company is also a tenant. It uses ground leases, where it leases the land and generally owns the building, and improved leases, where it leases land and building. Renewal options are typically its choice. Escalations can be fixed, inflation-linked, or market resets. Then it turns around and collects rent from the conventional franchisee, with a floor that parallels its own obligations. The key rack in the lease office is a map of that sandwich of leases. Why would an operator accept this? Because the site is the business. A drive-thru on a corner you cannot move is worth more than a royalty holiday on a weak lot. The Corporation's own risk section says the same thing in reverse. If it does not manage the real estate portfolio, operating results can suffer. Trade areas change. Digital and delivery change how people arrive. A 20-year site is a bet that the corner still matters. The filing also says the Company generally does not work with passive investors. It wants operators, not silent coupons. That is a culture sentence with an economic job. A passive investor wants the brand. An operator But why does that change the invoice? lives inside the rent envelope. If the operator cannot grow sales, the variable rent and the royalty sag, and the 10-K says restaurant margins arise from those fees and, to a lesser degree, from Company-operated sales. Headquarters needs the operator to be good at the window. The operator needs headquarters to keep the corner. When the 20 years end, the key is not a souvenir. It is a reset. A tired operator can be replaced without the Corporation inventing a new address. A strong operator can buy another term. A bad corner can be closed. That optionality is part of the fatter check. Rent is not only this year's percent of sales. Rent is the right to put a new name on the same dirt. The numbered key returns in this video for a reason. If you take it out, But why does that change the invoice? you have a spreadsheet. If you keep it, you have a machine a child can retell. Someone else cooks. Someone else pays crew. Headquarters keeps the key and sends the thicker envelope.

levels.name: The License Without Dirt
beats: Now the map splits. Not every McDonald's restaurant sits on Company-controlled dirt. Under a developmental license or affiliate arrangement, the 10-K says licensees are responsible for operating, managing, providing capital including the real estate interest, and opening new restaurants. The Company generally does not invest restaurant capital. It receives a royalty based on a percent of sales, and generally initial fees. That is a different invoice. There is no fatter rent stack from a building the Corporation does not control. The brand check still arrives. The key often does not. Look at the restaurant count again. International Developmental Licensed Markets and Corporate had 20,805 restaurants at year-end 2025. That count is bigger than the United States 13,706 and bigger than the International Operated Markets 10,845. About 99 percent of that developmental bucket was franchised. A huge share of the world's arches sit on a royalty-only deal. This is why a lazy "they are a real estate company" sentence fails, because the filing splits the map. That means a huge slice of the count is a license, not a landlord deal. In a large slice of the map, they are a licensor. The 2025 outlook expected developmental licensees and affiliates to put capital toward more than 1,800 openings in 2026, while the U.S. and International Operated Markets would open about 750. The Corporation's own 2026 capital plan of 3.7 to 3.9 billion dollars is aimed mostly at the markets where it still wants to plant keys. The rest of the globe can grow on other people's dirt. Why accept a thinner invoice? Because capital is finite, legal rules differ, and some markets are easier to grow when a local licensee owns the site. The filing says the optimal ownership structure depends on entrepreneurial talent, money, and local law around property and franchising. That is not poetry. It is why the map has two colors. The risk flips with the color. On conventional dirt, a weak operator can be swapped and the corner remains. On licensed dirt, the Corporation holds the brand and the contract, not the deed. If a licensee stumbles, headquarters does not automatically keep the building. The 10-K's franchisee-risk language applies to both, but the collateral is different. For the guest, the bag does not change. For the invoice, it changes everything. A developmental sale still feeds Systemwide sales and still feeds a royalty. It does not feed the 10.442 billion rent stack the same way. If you tell this story as one global landlord, you are mixing the colors. Hold the two invoices side by side. Conventional: lease plus license, rent plus royalty, key comes back in 20 years. Developmental: license, royalty, licensee brought the dirt. Same tray. Different envelope. The video has to show both or it is a poster.

levels.name: The Lab Kitchens
beats: Why keep any Company-operated restaurants at all? They look like the expensive way to sell fries. In fiscal 2025 they produced 9.690 billion dollars of recorded sales and 1.422 billion dollars of restaurant-level margin, after 8.268 billion of restaurant expenses. Inflation in food and labor hits this fleet in the face. The 2025 discussion says Company-operated margins reflected ongoing inflationary pressure in the United States and the International Operated Markets, and the U.S. fleet also had negative sales performance for the year. So the lab loses the glamour contest. It still has a job. The 10-K says Company restaurants let the Company improve operations across the System, test franchisee ideas, train people, and refine standards, marketing, products, and pricing. They are a school that happens to serve lunch. They also keep headquarters honest. If a new assembly step is stupid, the But why does that change the invoice? Company feels it in payroll before it forces it onto 40,000 operators. About 5 percent of restaurants, if you take the worldwide 95 percent franchised figure as the complement, are this lab and leftover owned fleet. The exact owned count is the remainder after the franchised percentage, and the filing does not need us to invent a headcount beyond that. The economic point is the mix. A small share of restaurants produces a large share of recorded sales because those sales are booked at the full ticket. A large share of restaurants produces a huge share of margin because those sales are booked as rent and royalty. That accounting costume fools people who only read the revenue line. Company-operated sales are 9.690 billion next to 16.548 billion of franchised revenue, so a careless glance says the owned stores are more But why does that change the invoice? than a third of the business. Then you look at restaurant margin dollars and the owned stores are about 10 percent. Then you look at Systemwide sales and the owned stores are about 7 percent of the 139.4 billion. Three different cameras. Only one of them is the guest's tray. Only one of them is the invoice. Only one of them is the lab. The lab also explains a choice that looks sentimental and is not. Selling every last Company restaurant would shrink the 9.690 billion line and could raise the blended operating margin. It would also shrink the place where the Corporation learns to be a franchisor. The filing treats that learning as a strength of the model. We do not have to romanticize it. We do have to leave it in the picture, or the 5 percent looks But why does that change the invoice? like a mistake. In the second quarter of 2026, Company-operated sales were still there, 2.525 billion next to 4.393 billion of franchised revenue. The lab did not vanish because loyalty users grew. Nearly 220 million 90-day loyalty users is a marketing fact. It does not flip the 90 percent franchised-margin share. The kitchen clipboard and the rent envelope can exist in the same company. They are not the same object. If this chapter feels quieter than the envelope chapter, that is the point. The lab is necessary and not the engine. A video that spends 12 minutes on fryers has followed the costume again.

levels.name: Why The Invoice Survives
beats: Copycats can sell burgers. Copycats can even franchise. The hard part is building an invoice that looks like this one without 20 years of keys. Start with density. A conventional corner with a drive-thru is a habit. The 2025 report calls the drive-thru network a competitive advantage and says the vast majority of new openings in the U.S. and International Operated Markets will include one. Habits are not moats by themselves. Habits plus a deed, or a 20-year lease the Corporation controls, are harder to lift. Add co-investment. The franchisee has already paid for equipment and decor. Walking away is not a mood. It is abandoning a room full of steel that does not move with you. Headquarters did not have to finance that steel. It still benefits when the operator needs the room to stay busy. Add the floor rent. But why does that change the invoice? A percent-of-sales royalty alone rides the week. A minimum rent paralleling the Company's own site costs keeps a pulse even when the window is soft. Combined with variable rent, the invoice can rise in good years without giving away the floor in bad ones. That mix is specific. It is not a motivational poster. Add standards. The Company says it requires rigorous standards and generally avoids passive investors. Brand damage at one restaurant is a System problem. The 10-K's legal section even mentions disputes over quality, service, cleanliness, delinquent rent, and franchise renewals. The invoice only works if the bag stays recognizable. Discipline is not a side quest. It is how 45,000 restaurants can share one guest expectation. Add scale that is not just store count. Fiscal 2025 openings and the 2026 plan toward roughly 2,600 openings and a 50,000-unit But why does that change the invoice? target by the end of 2027 are a construction program. Developmental licensees carry a lot of that capital. Conventional markets still get Company capital aimed at new keys. A rival can announce franchisees. A rival cannot instantly recreate 31.451 billion of contracted minimum rent or 22.8 billion of net property under franchise arrangements. What a rival can do is skip the dirt. Plenty of franchise systems collect a royalty and let the operator own the site. That can grow fast. It usually does not grow a rent stack that beats the royalty stack. If you are watching this to steal a model, steal the right object. The object is the key, not the mascot. The weakness belongs in the same chapter as the moat, or the video starts cheering. Franchisee health is the fuel. If franchisee sales worsen, the 10-K But why does that change the invoice? says financial results can be hurt, and it may be material. Headquarters does not magically print rent from a dead till. Company-operated inflation is a second crack. The owned fleet feels wage and food spikes that the franchised margin line does not feel the same way. Real estate inflexibility is a third. A 20-year corner can go wrong. Guest counts can stall even when prices rise. The second quarter of 2026 showed global comparable sales of only 1.3 percent, with the United States at 0.8 percent. An invoice can stay thick while the window feels tired. That tiredness still matters, because operators live in it. Loyalty growth is a patch, not a pardon. 40 billion dollars of trailing loyalty Systemwide sales means the app is catching repeats. It does not mean the guest has become the Corporation's customer. The guest But why does that change the invoice? is still paying the operator. The operator is still paying the envelope. Office cost is another costume. The 2025 outlook treated selling, general and administrative expenses as about 2.2 percent of Systemwide sales, not as a percent of the 26.885 billion. Headquarters spends to support a 139.4 billion system. It collects on the invoice. Those are different percentages on purpose.

levels.name: Who Signs
beats: So how does McDonald's really make money? Not by ringing every tray. Not by pretending a 46.1 percent operating margin is a tax on lunch. Not by a grocery license, and not by a loyalty badge. The Corporation books about 19 dollars of revenue per 100 dollars of Systemwide sales, on the fiscal 2025 mix. Inside the franchised slice, the thicker check is the rent, not the royalty. Conventional operators pay to use a site the Company generally controls, on a clock that is generally 20 years, and the key comes back. Developmental licensees pay a royalty and bring their own dirt. A small Company-operated fleet still rings full tickets so headquarters can stay a credible franchisor. About 90 percent of restaurant margin dollars in fiscal 2025, and again in the second quarter of 2026, came from the franchised side. The But why does that change the invoice? guest is real. The guest is not the customer on the invoice. The person who signs the 20-year lease is. If you want to know whether next year will be a good year for the listed company, do not only watch the bag at the window. Watch whether operators can still pay the thicker envelope. The numbered key goes back on the rack. The tray keeps moving. Those are not the same motion. If you remember one pair of numbers after the credits, remember 10.442 and 6.018, fiscal 2025, rents and royalties, same 10-K table. If you remember one object, remember the key. If you remember one customer, remember the person who signed. That is how McDonald's really makes money. Not a vibe. A stack of invoices with a deed underneath the conventional ones. A rival burger system can grow But why does that change the invoice? on royalty alone and let someone else keep the keys. That is a different invoice, and it is a different video. This one ends on the envelope.
A rival burger franchise that lets the operator keep more of the dirt would have to explain a thinner envelope. That title is waiting if this one holds.
